title: Divisibility tests and modular remainders
transcript: A remainder measures how far a number is past a multiple. A remainder just one below the divisor tells you the number is one step before the next multiple. That one step can turn several awkward remainders into a single common multiples problem.

In AMC practice, read almost full groups and one short of a multiple as clues about a remainder. In a Rossmoyne style search, combine more than one remainder and use the interval to finish the argument.
Group fifty-one counters into packets of six. How many counters remain outside full packets? Identify the last multiple of the packet size that fits. Then count the ungrouped counters.

eight packets use forty-eight counters. The next packet would bring the used total above fifty-one. Subtract to get three. The leftover amount is less than the group size, as a valid remainder must be.
Find the last digit of the three-digit number beginning with four and six if the number is divisible by four and three. Use the last two digits for one test and the digit sum for the other.

The possible endings divisible by four are sixty, sixty-four and sixty-eight, so the last digit is zero, four or eight. The fixed digits sum to ten. Of those three last digits, only eight makes a multiple of three. The number is four hundred and sixty-eight. Its ending and its digit sum pass the two requested tests.

Count the numbers from sixty-three through two hundred and twenty-two whose remainder is four on division by five. The same numbers must give remainder seven on division by eight. What happens to both remainders if you add one?

Adding one to N makes it divisible by five and eight. Their least common multiple is forty. The shifted interval starts at sixty-four and ends at two hundred and twenty-three. Find the first and last multiples of forty in that interval. They start at eighty and finish at two hundred. Step by forty, including both ends.

There are three steps between the endpoints. Include the first multiple to get four numbers. Subtract one from each multiple to recover the original numbers. For example, the first is seventy-nine and gives both required remainders.

A remainder can be zero, but it must always be smaller than the divisor. Once there are enough leftovers for a complete group, make that group. When you shift the number in a bounded search, shift the endpoints by the same amount. Pull each answer back to the original interval.

Name the divisor and the remainder together. Check whether adding or subtracting a small amount lands on a multiple. Check the first and last values against every condition. If you counted gaps, include the first valid value.
